Package com.github.tommyettinger.cringe

Class WangTiler

java.lang.Object
com.github.tommyettinger.cringe.WangTiler
public final class WangTiler extends Object
A utility class that allows finding the appropriate index of Wang-tiling or omni-tiling regions to place on a grid. This allows an int seed to produce many possible tilings for the same region in space. It can lay out Wang tiling square areas with select(int, int, int), cubes with select(int, int, int, int), and so on up to 6D. It can lay out single-edge (omni-tiling) square areas with selectSingleEdge(int, int, int), but can also use selectSingleEdgeSeparated(int, int, int) or selectSingleEdgeAlternate(int, int, int) in 2D. In 3D and higher dimensions, you can use selectSingleEdge(int, int, int, int) and its overloads.

  • Method Details

    • select

      public static int select(int x, int y, int seed)
      Allows determining which index in a Wang-tiling set of squares, from 0 to 15 inclusive, to place at a given point on a grid with a configurable seed. This expects the noise indices to match what WangNoiseGenerator uses, that is, what WangContinuousNoise.setWangTile2D(int, WangRawNoise) uses as well. This considers positive x to be a movement to the east (rightward), and positive y to be a movement to the south (downward).
      Parameters:
      x - horizontal grid position to place a Wang-tiling square
      y - vertical grid position to place a Wang-tiling square; uses y-down by default
      seed - can be any int, but should be the same for a single tiling space
      Returns:
      an index between 0 and 15, inclusive, referring to what index does in WangContinuousNoise.setWangTile2D(int, WangRawNoise)

    • selectSingleEdge

      public static int selectSingleEdge(int x, int y, int seed)
      Gets a pseudo-random index from 0 to 63, inclusive, for single-edge (omni-tiling) 2D noise. This is likely to choose some index more than once given 9 or more tiles.
      Parameters:
      x - horizontal grid position to place a Wang-tiling square
      y - vertical grid position to place a Wang-tiling square; y-up or y-down doesn't matter here
      seed - all bits are used; should be the same for a single tiling space
      Returns:
      an index between 0 and 63, inclusive

    • selectSingleEdgeSeparated

      public static int selectSingleEdgeSeparated(int x, int y, int seed)
      Gets a less-random index from 0 to 63, inclusive, for single-edge (omni-tiling) noise. This won't repeat in the first 8x8 grid of tiles, which can be useful to reduce the appearance of duplicates. This only can take x and y from 0 to 65535 meaningfully. Only the low 12 bits of seed are used, so seeds from 0 to 4095 will all work, but higher ones will be duplicates. This uses the Rosenberg-Strong pairing function, which lines up indices in concentric squares. See Steven Pigeon's blog for more on that.
      Parameters:
      x - non-negative horizontal grid position to place a Wang-tiling square
      y - non-negative vertical grid position to place a Wang-tiling square; y-up or y-down doesn't matter here
      seed - only the low 12 bits are used; should be the same for a single tiling space
      Returns:
      an index between 0 and 63, inclusive

    • selectSingleEdgeAlternate

      public static int selectSingleEdgeAlternate(int x, int y, int seed)
      Gets a less-random index from 0 to 63, inclusive, for single-edge (omni-tiling) noise. This shouldn't repeat in the first 6x6 grid of tiles, which can be useful to reduce the appearance of duplicates. This only can take x and y from 0 to 65535 meaningfully. Only the low 12 bits of seed are used, so seeds from 0 to 4095 will all work, but higher ones will be duplicates. This uses the Cantor pairing function, which lines up indices in right-triangle shapes. See Steven Pigeon's blog for more on that.
      Parameters:
      x - non-negative horizontal grid position to place a Wang-tiling square
      y - non-negative vertical grid position to place a Wang-tiling square; y-up or y-down doesn't matter here
      seed - only the low 12 bits are used; should be the same for a single tiling space
      Returns:
      an index between 0 and 63, inclusive
